1:
Henry, and Wesley almost word for word after him, takes the title as an office. God clothes Moses with great power in making him a god to Pharaoh, that is, his representative in this affair, as magistrates are called gods because they are God's vicegerents; he was authorised to act in God's name, endued with power to do what is above the ordinary course of nature, and invested with authority to demand obedience of a sovereign prince. Yet Henry marks the limits carefully: it was a made deity, not one held essentially by nature, and none but by commission; and it reached only to Pharaoh, whereas the living and true God is God to all the world. It is an instance of God's condescension that when he treats with men he treats by men, whose terror shall not make us afraid. Aaron is then named as an assistant, not a man of uncircumcised lips but a notable spokesman, who shall be his prophet — that is, shall speak from him to Pharaoh as prophets do from God to men — so that Moses as a god shall inflict and remove the plagues, and Aaron as a prophet denounce them.

Calvin reads the words as a remedy for the anxiety and unbelief the prophet had shown: the title means he was furnished with supreme authority, whereby he should cast down the tyrant's pride. But God took nothing from himself to transfer it to Moses, since he so communicates to his servants what is peculiar to himself as to remain himself in his completeness; when he seems to resign a part of his glory to his ministers, he only teaches that the efficacy of his Spirit will be joined with their labours, that these may not be fruitless. He was a god to Pharaoh because in him God exerted his power, that he should be superior to the greatness of the king; and it is a common figure of the Hebrews to give the title to all things excellent. By this consolation his weakness was supported, so that relying on God's authority he might fearlessly despise the fierceness of the king. The name of prophet is used here for an interpreter, since that office proceeds from God alone; and because God delivered through the one to the other what he wished said, Aaron is made subject to his brother as if to God himself. This is clearer in the verse following, where the power granted is circumscribed: in directing him to speak whatever he commands, God ranks him as a minister and confines him under authority, without departing from his own rights.

Ellicott takes the whole as God's answer to the objection about uncircumcised lips, probably following it at once. The force of it is that Moses is not called on to speak but to act: in action he will be as a god, powerful, wonder-working, irresistible, while his brother, who is eloquent, must do the speaking. Prophet he would render spokesman, the declarer of another's mind, which is the primary sense. Clarke says the same in a sentence — at his word every plague should come and at his command each be removed — and sets out the chapter's argument: the dignified mission of the two, the prediction that the king's heart should be hardened that God might multiply his signs, the rod turned into a serpent and imitated by the magicians, the threat at the river, the waters turned to blood, and the plague enduring seven days. Gill notes that the answer meets an objection taken from his own meanness and the majesty of Pharaoh. Keil observes that the word rendered armies is used of Israel leaving Egypt equipped and organised by tribes, to contend for the cause of the Lord and fight his battles — in which respect they are called the hosts of Jehovah.
3:
Calvin observes that the expression is harsh, and that many commentators take pains to soften it. Some join the clauses so that the multiplying of signs becomes the external cause of the obstinacy; but Moses has already declared, and repeats afterwards, that the king's mind was made stubborn in other ways besides the working of miracles. Calvin's own rendering is adversative — I indeed will harden his heart, but I will multiply my signs — as though it were said that the hardness will be no obstacle, since the wonders suffice to overcome it. He does not reject the alternative that God willed the resistance so that the deliverance might be more conspicuous. What he will not allow is the reduction of the whole to a bare permission: they are but poor speculators who refer it there, since in blinding minds God inflicts a deserved punishment, not merely leaving men to do as they please but executing a judgment he knows to be just, and delivering to Satan those deserving of such blindness. The blame nevertheless rests with the men themselves, who with a willfulness like madness rush into sin; and those who pretend that God is thus made the author of evil confuse two different things, for the hardness of heart is the sin of man, but the hardening of the heart is the judgment of God. It is absurd, he adds, to measure incomprehensible judgments by the little scale of our own apprehension.

Clarke gives the softer construction without argument: God will permit the stubbornness still to remain, that he may have the greater opportunity to multiply his wonders in the land. Gill passes the clause over to his own earlier note, and Ellicott likewise refers back to the fourth chapter, adding a distinction among the terms. Signs were miracles done as credentials, proving a mission; wonders were miracles generally; a third word, also rendered wonders, denotes those wrought in the way of punishment, elsewhere called judgments. That last term returns at once in the promise of great judgments. On the syntax Ellicott is careful: the Hebrew is not that the king shall not hearken so that God may lay on his hand, but that he will not hearken, and God will lay it on. No relation of effect and cause is asserted between the two clauses, which are co-ordinate. The armies and the people are likewise not two things but one, the phrases standing in apposition, the second explaining the first. Gill takes the announcement pastorally, as told beforehand lest the brothers be discouraged and conclude their labour vain.

The stated end is knowledge in the Egyptians, and Ellicott presses how much that meant. To know the name is to know that its bearer answers to it, the only really existing God, the so-called gods of Egypt being vapour, smoke, nothingness. Egypt was then the greatest monarchy in the world and at the height of her glory; among existing polytheisms hers was the most famous, and her deities must have seemed to her neighbours the most powerful, so that to discredit them was to discredit polytheism generally. Calvin hears a species of irony in the promise, since the acknowledgment is extorted from the unwilling: they oppose an iron obstinacy to every threatening until violence forces them into alarm, not humbled but merely unable to escape punishment — like drunkards roused from their stupor who would gladly sleep on, yet must bear the pains of their intemperance. Such men so know God that, lost in shame and fear, they see not what they do see. Clarke reads the permitted opposition as mercy to Egypt, that the departure might be so signal that the Almighty should appear all-sufficient; and Keil marks the shape of the section, which opens with a sign attesting the commission and closes with the last blow announced, the nine plagues at its centre.
6:
Calvin notes that it is not for boasting that the historian records his own compliance: having confessed his earlier hesitation, he now relates that the two were in better courage for their office, bringing no talent or dexterity of their own but simply obeying. As we may attempt nothing except what God prescribes, so we ought without objection to pursue whatever he commands. Ellicott marks the same turn: from here the resistance ceases, the leader subdues his own will and earns the praise of being faithful as a servant in all God's house, while his brother's obedience continues until Sinai, where it failed before the frenzy of the people. Gill adds that afterwards they never objected to any errand, but set about it cheerfully.

The ages that follow are, in Calvin's reading, an amplification. It was no common case that two octogenarians should engage actively in so difficult a charge; and he will not join those who think their years merely enhanced their dignity. The point is rather that, excluding all human means, the glory might be celebrated of a God who performed so mighty a work by men failing and decrepit, who might themselves have been timid and troubled the people, being leaders not far from the grave. Clarke does the arithmetic: forty years before Midian and forty in Midian, the elder brother three years the senior. Ellicott observes that the air of Egypt, and still more of the desert, favoured long life, the monuments showing officials employed past a hundred. Wesley draws the contrast with Joseph, who was to be only a servant to Pharaoh and was preferred at thirty, whereas the man who was to be a god to Pharaoh waited till eighty: fit that such honour be long awaited and such service long prepared for. Gill takes the tally as marking how long the affliction had run.

The demand for a sign is anticipated before it is made. Henry observes that the first approach produced only the instructions; now the credentials are called for. It is taken for granted that the king will challenge the demandants to work something evidently above the power of nature, and so prove a commission from the God of nature — yet he asks with no desire to be convinced, hoping nothing will be wrought and he may then have colour for his infidelity. Clarke defines the word as an effect opposed to the laws of nature, or such as her powers are inadequate to produce; and it has ever been the sense of mankind that one sent on so singular an errand can give supernatural evidence of it. Ellicott suspects the king had heard of the signs wrought before Israel and was curious to witness one, as Herod was later; or expected his own magicians to show greater, and so dismiss the brothers as impostors. Calvin finds this usual with unbelievers: they demand proofs of power which they may still discredit, not professedly scorning God but urged by secret impiety to seek subterfuges; direct refusal not being dared, a pretext is invented, and when the sign is given they seek deeper lurking places. Henry follows the contest through: the staff that was to signal every later wonder is itself made the subject of one, to put a reputation upon it; serpents are dreadful creatures, and the sight might have softened the king into fear, so that though no plague it amounted to the threat of one. The imitation by the magicians drained the conviction away, whether their rods became serpents by permitted delusion or by evil angels substituting; but the swallowing settled it, great truth prevailing. The rod is called Aaron's now because entrusted to him, and Keil argues it is the same wondrous staff of the fourth chapter, since the one held over the waters afterwards must be the one turned into a serpent here.
10:
Calvin observes that even men conscious of their vocation and armed with power for wonders would never have dared approach so fierce a tyrant, had not the inward inspiration of the Spirit steeled them to persevere, raising them by faith above everything lofty on earth. Gill has them entering the palace boldly, clothed with authority and assured of success. On the usual question whether the change of the staff was substantial, Calvin is confident that it was: there is no more difficulty with God in changing the forms of things than in creating heaven and earth out of nothing,; since this one ran contrary to nature's course we must judge of it as of the pillar of salt, save that the staff soon returned to its first form. Clarke is exercised by the noun. The word here is not the one used at the burning bush but the term elsewhere rendered whale, dragon or sea-monster, used of some very large creature, aquatic or amphibious; some have thought the crocodile is meant. The objection that a staff and a common snake are of comparable size he sets aside, since a miracle was being wrought, and it was as easy to change a rod into a crocodile as into an adder.

The court answers with its own professionals, whose three names are pressed by several hands. Clarke renders them men of learning, revealers of hidden things — diviners who claimed to uncover the future and find things lost — and decipherers of abstruse writings; the word for their enchantments he traces to a root meaning to burn, supposing rites of lustral fires, fumigations and aromatic drugs by which assistant spirits were evoked. Ellicott gives them as wise men, mutterers of charms, and scribes or writers of charms, and describes how widely the art was practised there: a large part of the Ritual of the Dead is charms for the soul to utter in Hades to pass the monsters it would meet, other works survive as mere collections of magical receipts. He notes the Jewish tradition, taken up by Paul, which named two of them, one famous enough to be named by Pliny and Apuleius. Calvin remarks the courtesy of the title: they are honourably called wise men though inventors of deceit, for though astronomy flourished among them, their degenerate science was vanity — as Satan, to appropriate God's glory or appear an angel of light, conceals falsehood under specious titles. Gill calls them jugglers who cast a mist before people's eyes.

Whether real creatures lay on that floor divides them. Ellicott thinks the men merely knew secrets of nature not generally known and were trained in sleight of hand, and suggests the trick familiar to Egyptian serpent-charmers in every age, by which a charmed reptile is made to look like a stick and then disenchanted. Clarke argues the opposite: if they became serpents after being thrown down, dexterity had nothing to do with it, the rods being out of their hands, and no nimbleness accounts for one devouring the rest. Calvin allows that the king's eyes may have been deceived, yet finds nothing absurd in saying such liberty was conceded — not to create one body out of another, but to set forth God's work as their own — the potency of error far surpassing our comprehension, and given, as Paul says, that those who will not obey the truth should believe a lie. Either way the swallowing was decisive, and Calvin presses how the king failed to see it: the wicked maliciously close their eyes against manifested power. Ellicott insists the closing verb is intransitive and the received clause a mistranslation — his heart hardened itself — since a final penal hardening requires that in the earlier stages the man be left to himself. Clarke says the same; Wesley compresses it to permission.
14:
The word reported to Moses is not the one used for a stiffening but for a weight: Gill renders it heavy, dull and stupid, so that the king cannot lift up his heart to obey. Clarke reads it the same way — no conviction is received, for all the clearness of the light shining on him — and adds what we know of prejudice: where men are set on a predetermined plan, arguments, demonstrations and even miracles are lost upon them, as with the obstinate opponents of the apostles. Calvin sees in this single reprobate a picture of human pride wherever it is not controlled by tractableness, and warns the faithful against provoking a like vengeance, since the same Being who hardened him avenges impiety constantly, smiting his enemies with confusion and rendering them as furious as they are senseless. He also hears encouragement in the announcement: told the heart was hardened, the messenger might waver unless hope of victory were shown him, and so God arms his servant afresh, as if to say the beast must be worn down though it could not be broken. He adds, though some will think it far-fetched, that the ten plagues answer to the ten precepts, the wicked smitten with as many strokes as God was about to give commandments.

Both hour and place of the next meeting are chosen, and Keil insists neither is incidental. The king goes out in the morning to the river, not for an airing or to see how high the water had risen, but beyond doubt to present his daily worship to the Nile, which Egypt honoured as supreme deity; and at that moment God's will concerning Israel is declared to him. Henry reasons to the same spot from the other end: the messenger might not be admitted to the presence-chamber where ambassadors had audience, and so is sent to the bank, where God foresaw the king would come — for thus all people will walk, every one in the name of his god, and none fail to worship in the morning. There the summons is renewed and, on refusal, judgment announced upon the water they stood beside — beforehand, lest any call it chance or lay it to another cause, and that it might appear done by the power of the God of the Hebrews as punishment for obstinacy; and the rod is expressly carried, that the king might be alarmed at the staff which had lately triumphed over those of his own men.

Henry weighs the stroke under three heads. It was dreadful: nothing is more common than water, so kindly has Providence ordered that what is needful to life be cheap and everywhere had, yet now Egypt must drink blood or die of thirst, and the fish that were much of their food died, the land made loathsome by the stench. It was righteous, for the river was their idol, served above the Creator; God turned into blood what they had turned into a god — that creature which we idolize he justly removes or embitters, making a scourge of what we set up as a competitor. They had also stained that water with the blood of Hebrew children, and now had blood to drink; none ever thirsted after it but sooner or later had enough. And it was significant, since Egypt so depended on the river that smiting it warned of ruin running through every product of the land until it reached the firstborn, the red stream a direful omen of the Red Sea. He closes with a comparison: one of the first miracles here was water turned to blood, one of the first wrought by our Lord water turned to wine; for the law came by Moses, a dispensation of death and terror, while grace and truth, which like wine make glad the heart, came by Jesus Christ.
15:
Gill notes the hour: the next morning, when the mind is most composed, fit to attend to what is suggested. Why the king should be at the water at all is variously guessed. Clarke thinks it probably for bathing or some religious washing, and cites the report that nothing stood in greater honour among the Egyptians than their river; he passes on too the older Jewish supposition that the king was himself a magician, walking out each morning to prepare his rites. Ellicott offers the bathing too, recalling the princess who drew the infant from the reeds, or else some festival in the river's honour, of which the calendar held several; and he renders the place of waiting literally, the lip of the river. The staff that had become a serpent is to be in hand, and the message delivered with name and title in full — for at the first application the king had professed not to know who Jehovah was, and to prevent his saying so again both are given. The complaint that follows is not that he had not listened but that he had not obeyed.

The sign is announced to the same end as before, that he should know the name; and Ellicott notes how the smiting is claimed. The rod in my hand means in the hand of my servant, God representing himself as about to do what was in fact done by another — he who acts through another acts himself. Clarke marks this as the opening of the series and reproduces a chronology placing all ten within one month: blood on the eighteenth of the sixth month, frogs on the twenty-fifth, lice on the twenty-seventh, flies on the twenty-ninth, murrain on the second of the seventh, boils, hail and locusts within the week, darkness on the tenth of Abib, and the firstborn slain on the fifteenth. He sets his own caution against it: most of these dates are destitute of proof. Gill takes the promised knowledge plainly, as coming by an instance of power and vengeance.

The threatened loathing is what Clarke dwells on, quoting at length to make its force felt, since nothing carries here without knowing how pleasant and wholesome that water was reckoned. One traveller reports it so delicious that one would not wish the heat less, nor be delivered from thirst; that the Turks found it so exquisite they ate salt to make themselves drink more; that Egyptians abroad spoke of nothing but the pleasure of drinking it at their return, preferring that to the sight of their families; that a man tasting it first can scarcely believe it is not prepared by art, and that it should rank among waters as champagne among wines. Its best quality was that it never incommoded, however much was taken, some drinking three buckets a day — and this of the river only, their well water being detestable, fountains a kind of prodigy, and rain out of the question. Another adds that whoever has not heard this will never have felt the energy of the threat: they shall loathe the water they preferred to all the waters of the world, and choose rather the wells they abhorred. Ellicott supplies the other half of the loss. The river's natural discolorations, by red earth or minute organisms, harm the fish nothing and leave the water fit for use; but the fish were a large part of the people's subsistence, so that to lose them was severe, with implied contempt of their religion besides, three species at least being sacred. Gill puts the reason simply: their element was changed and they could live in no other. The stench he will not explain away by the river's occasional natural odour, too slight for what is meant here, when waters like blood and laden with putrid fish caused a disgust not to be spoken.
19:
The command reaches every kind of water in the country, and Ellicott sets out what that meant: the main stream, its branches, the canals drawn from it, the ponds left by the inundation, and the reservoirs in gardens, courts and houses. There is no other stream in the land, and no natural springs or brooks; water can be had by digging, but the soil is impregnated with nitre and the well water unpalatable. This verse, he adds, shows a very exact knowledge of that system. The vessels of wood and stone he explains from the practice of storing river water in tanks to drop its sediment, such cisterns standing in all the better houses. Clarke reads the clause more simply, as extending the stroke to water already carried indoors; he mentions the suggestion that the two vessels refer instead to filtering that thick water through pots of white earth, but prefers the plain sense.

Calvin asks why this stroke came first, answering from what the river was to Egypt. Great wealth, defence and convenience arose from it: the fisheries, the fertility of a country watered by its overflow — a thing injurious elsewhere — the navigation, and the fortification it made for much of the kingdom. To cast them down from their chief dependence, its waters are turned to blood; and since water is one of the two elements of which our life consists, to take away one part of life was the shortest way of humbling them, had they not been wholly intractable. God might by a single breath have dried up every source and overwhelmed them with drought, but that would have been thought chance or nature, a less apparent prodigy, and would have shut up the way for the rest. The listing of streams and ponds follows because the river was so diffused, by art and nature, that scarcely any country is so supplied — as if to say the store shall avail nothing, for they shall thirst as though the Nile were dry, and in whatever vessel they drew would find only blood. Wesley, repeating the charge that the river was served above the Creator, turns it to use: every creature is to us what he makes it, water or blood; what is water today may be blood tomorrow, and what is vain may soon become vexatious — for it is sin that turns our waters into blood.

Gill has the staff handed over and the brother going to the water side; Ellicott is certain the lifter is Aaron. He dwells on who watched: if the day was a festival of the river, the king would have gone out attended by the officers of the court, priests and vast numbers of people; if merely for bathing, he would still have had a train. Either way the sign was public. Clarke insists the change was real and not in appearance only, the water becoming corrupt, so that the fish died and the smell grew offensive. Gill argues the same from the fish: had it only worn the colour of blood they would have lived as before; and the loss touched Egypt less in drink than in food, fish being what the common people lived on, the stink coming of blood corrupting in the heat with dead fish floating on it. Ellicott marks a small advance in the wording: before they had loathed to drink, yet apparently drank; now they could not, the draught being too nauseous. Calvin observes that the counsellors saw it too, which argues the same infatuation through the court; and it marked the nation's reprobation that out of all that multitude none laboured to correct the king's folly. So God confounds the wisdom of the world, for no nation gloried more in its universal knowledge, as Isaiah reproached them; yet, proud and amazed by turns, they betrayed not a spark of sound intelligence.
22:
If every water was blood, on what did the court's men work? Clarke answers from the digging that follows: pits were sunk along the river, and that water was not bloody. He adds that though the commission covered streams and pools, only the river is said to have been smitten at first, so other water lay ready for imitation, to which juggling or a familiar spirit could give a bloody look and a fetid smell. Ellicott makes the imitation poor beside the original: the brothers had changed river, canals, lakes and reservoirs, while the court's men could only work on some small quantity, reddening it or substituting blood by sleight of hand, with no test applied and no hostile witness — enough, though, to let the king harden himself. Calvin supposes clear water appeared for a little while and was then changed, God opening a way for himself until the contests reached their end; the notion that they fetched it from the dwellings of Israel he calls forced. Whether the change was true or imaginary he dare not decide, except that it accords better with satanic delusion that the eyes of the wicked were deceived, as Paul says God sends error to those who refuse the truth. Wesley and Gill note how mean it was: could they have turned the bloody river back to water they would have equalled the miracle; to spoil a little good water was unworthy.

Clarke reads the stroke as retributive. That river had been made the grave of the Hebrew male children by the murderous decree, and now the water necessary to their own life was deadly; and since a girl — some say a boy and a girl — was yearly sacrificed to it in gratitude, the contempt poured on it tended to correct their notions and bring them to own the true God. The king was untouched. Ellicott is careful with the idiom: he did not set his heart — pay attention — even to this, but passed it over as a slight matter and went home; care was probably taken to keep him supplied from the wells, brackish though they were, sufficient for his customary washings, while he drank a more generous liquid. Calvin fastens on the clause as proof that the hardness was voluntary and the sin his own, God's secret appointment availing nothing to lessen his blame: blinded by pride, he took no account of the glory before him. So the wicked, though cast into a reprobate mind, still harden themselves, running against God willfully, and their audacity takes away the excuse of ignorance — which warns us not to slumber when God arouses us.

Ellicott explains the digging. Wells sunk anywhere in the alluvium always yield water, brackish and unpalatable, drawn by percolation from the river; but percolation is slow, and blood would scarcely travel far by it, so what they reached was probably in the ground already and never subject to the sign. Calvin finds in the digging, and more in the seven days, an increase of certainty: had the corruption been momentary some suspicion of trickery might have crept in, which the continued taste and appearance removed. Ellicott takes the week as its duration, lengthened because no submission was made: having water enough for himself, the king thought little of its continuance. Gill dates it from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth of the sixth month, and observes that no request for its removal is recorded, though one ancient writer says otherwise; it was lifted unasked. Clarke, weighing why God should contend with such men at all, passes on four reasons: that they be let exert their utmost, lest the wonders be laid to magic; that wavering Israel might see the difference; that they be afterwards safe from false signs; and, in mercy to Egypt, that the gods they trusted be seen unable to undo one plague.
